content.p: On 21 March 1960 South African police opened fire on a crowd that had gathered outside the police station in Sharpeville, a township about 70 km south of Johannesburg. The people had come to protest the pass laws, which required black South Africans to carry a passbook at all times. The police figures published in 1960 put the toll at 69 dead and about 180 wounded, and the Apartheid Museum still gives "at least 69" killed and 180 wounded. Historians who went back to police and national archives argue the real numbers were far higher.

The 1960 inquiry named no police shooter, and the criminal trial that followed was of Sharpeville residents. The event became shorthand for the violence of apartheid, brought a Security Council resolution within days and pushed the country's main African opposition movements underground.

EBSCO's research summary describes the passbook, or dompas, as a document holding its owner's fingerprints, photograph and information about which areas the owner could enter. Failing to carry it was grounds for immediate arrest. After the National Party came to power in 1948, the pass system sat inside a wider structure of racial classification and enforced residential segregation.

South African History Online records that at the African National Congress conference of 16 December 1959, Chief Albert Luthuli declared 1960 the "Year of the Pass", with a national anti-pass campaign planned to begin on 31 March. The Pan Africanist Congress, a breakaway from the ANC formed in 1959 under Robert Sobukwe, moved first. On 16 March Sobukwe told the Commissioner of Police that the PAC would protest the pass laws from 21 March. On 18 March circulars told Black South Africans to leave their passbooks at home and present themselves at police stations to be arrested, an attempt to clog the system. City Press writer David Forbes gives 19 March as the date of Sobukwe's call.

In Sharpeville the message arrived in letterboxes. Elizabeth Mabona, in her first public testimony to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, recalled that residents found notes telling them not to go to work on 21 March. The timeline adds that task forces had taken Sharpeville's bus drivers the previous evening, so even residents who wanted to work had no buses. On the morning itself, people on their way to work were stopped by activists heading for the police station and told to join them.

Historians Nancy Clark and William Worger, writing in The Conversation, say the police opened fire at about 1.40 in the afternoon on a crowd of about 4,000. They draw on testimony from the 1960 commission of enquiry and the criminal trial of over 70 residents, together with later claimants' statements. They write that the residents' testimony, including that of every African who worked for the municipality or as a police officer in Sharpeville, unanimously said the crowd gathered peacefully.

By the time of the shooting, according to those witnesses, almost 300 policemen had been moved into the township, at least 13 of the white officers carrying Sten machine guns, with five Saracen armoured vehicles. Clark and Worger say police testimony makes clear that the officer in charge gave the order to shoot, and that machine gunners fired into the crowd from no more than 3 to 5 metres away. One white official said the scene "made me think of a wheat field, where a whirlwind had shaken it." The crowd was taken by surprise, and over three quarters of the dead and injured were shot in the back as they ran.

EBSCO's account is more cautious about the trigger. It says the police were unnerved by the crowd and by a scuffle at a police-station gate, and that the shots set off a stampede. Forbes, writing in City Press, says nobody knows the exact trigger, that the firing lasted about 45 seconds, and that police claimed no command to shoot had been given while witnesses heard a policeman shout "skiet!" and another shout "vuur!". South African History Online likewise says witnesses positioned in front of the crowd saw a senior officer arrive moments before the shooting and give the order to fire.

Afterwards, the local commander, Colonel Pienaar, is quoted on the timeline as saying, "I don't know how many we shot", and that if crowds "do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way." Segametsi Mahkanya, who watched from a friend's window, told of police inspecting the dead and, in her words, putting stones and knives in dead people's hands. Forbes writes that witnesses described the commander ordering stones gathered into a fire bucket to suggest the crowd had thrown them. Forbes also reports that nearly all the bodies were removed within 20 minutes, before photographers who had hurried from Johannesburg could record them.

EBSCO reports 69 dead, among them eight women and ten children, and of the injured who could be identified, 39 women and 19 children. It says 52 of the dead were shot in the back, and that 77 of the injured were later arrested in their hospital beds. The UCLA Library, describing its collection of the inquiry and trial transcripts, says as many as 330 people were killed and wounded.

Clark and Worger challenge the official count directly. They say the police minimised the number of victims by at least a third and that their research raises the toll to at least 91 dead and 281 injured, against the official 69 and 180. Their sources include witness statements recorded from hospital beds in the days after the shooting and nearly 300 police-taken statements, some made under oath for the criminal case and some given voluntarily in 1961 and 1962 to support compensation claims that failed.

The same research is reported with different numbers elsewhere. Forbes, in City Press, says the police version was 69 dead and 178 injured and that the research shows at least 80 killed and 297 injured, a figure that does not include three unborn children lost to gunshot wounds suffered by their mothers. He describes Christina Motsepe, 19, shot in the back while looking for her mother, and Mamotshabi Malikoe, 21, who bled to death from a chest wound. He also names people who died later, including Sello Ralebakeng, who was hurt on 21 March and died in custody on 20 July when a truck carrying prisoners to trial crashed. The two articles do not agree on the totals, so the safest statement is that official figures of 69 killed are widely regarded by researchers as an undercount, with 80 and 91 both given for the revised toll.

Sharpeville was not the only place where police shot protesters that day. Al Jazeera reports that in Langa, near Cape Town, police opened fire and killed three people, wounding at least 26 others; a driver who had taken two journalists there was also killed. South African History Online says two protesters died, which is one of several differing counts for Langa.

On 22 March Prime Minister Verwoerd told Parliament that the protests had nothing to do with the pass laws, called them a "periodic phenomenon" and thanked the police for acting in a "courageous and efficient manner". The timeline records him as claiming that protesters had shot first. On 23 March Sobukwe, Kitchener Leballo and 11 other senior PAC figures were charged with incitement. The timeline records that Philip Kgosana, a young PAC activist in Cape Town, led a protest march from the African townships to the city centre on 23 March. Al Jazeera, which dates the march to 30 March, says some estimates put it at 30,000 to 50,000 people covering 15 km from Langa to Caledon Square police station, and that Kgosana was jailed and held in solitary confinement for 21 days.

The government banned gatherings of more than twelve people on 24 March. On 25 March representatives of 29 African and Asian states asked for an urgent Security Council meeting about "large-scale killings of unarmed and peaceful demonstrators". On 27 March the Commissioner of Police announced that pass laws were suspended, saying the reason was that the jails could no longer hold the many Africans presenting themselves for arrest. Luthuli announced he would burn his pass, and the ANC called a national stay-at-home on 28 March, when passbooks were burned across the country. South African History Online reports that more than 11 000 people were detained after the state of emergency on 30 March; EBSCO puts the figure at about eighteen thousand. On 1 April the Security Council adopted Resolution 134 calling on South Africa to abandon its apartheid policies, with nine in favour and France and the United Kingdom abstaining.
content.h2: Inquiry, trial and a law against suing
content.p: The government opened a Commission of Enquiry at once. The UCLA Library describes its purpose as, in large part, to identify organisations and individuals who could be held responsible and, above all, someone in the crowd who had fired first. The enquiry, run by Judge P. J. Wessels as its sole member, interviewed over 100 witnesses. His report absolved the police in the face of what it deemed a dangerous crowd and never named a responsible shooter, in the crowd or among the police.

The state also charged more than 70 Sharpeville residents in Regina v Monyake and others. According to the UCLA Library, 147 witnesses testified, 41 of them previously heard by the commission. Most defendants were found not guilty of public violence for lack of direct evidence, and five were convicted. EBSCO says Sobukwe received a three-year sentence for provoking the incident, and that a special amendment, the "Sobukwe clause", later allowed the police to detain him indefinitely without trial. The Apartheid Museum says he was imprisoned for nine years after his arrest on 21 March 1960.

When civil claims arose from the killings, EBSCO says, the government passed the Indemnity Act of 1961, which protected the state and its officials against claims arising from their actions during the crisis.

In April 1960 the ANC and PAC were banned and driven underground. The Apartheid Museum notes that both formed armed wings, the ANC's Umkhonto we Sizwe and the PAC's Poqo, and that by 1964 most of their internal leadership had been arrested, most famously in the Rivonia Trial. Emilia Potenza, curator of the museum, told Al Jazeera that a chance for peaceful negotiated change was lost. Abroad, according to EBSCO, the shooting increased calls for economic sanctions.

After 1994 the day was renamed Human Rights Day. Forbes argues that the name devalues what happened, and Al Jazeera quotes Shirley Gunn of the Langa Memorial Collective saying that burning passes was not the main point of Sharpeville. Clark and Worger note that the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, though it chose Sharpeville as the formal beginning of its investigation of apartheid crimes, heard only three witnesses from the community during part of one day. They say residents believe the neglect stems from the protest having been organised by the PAC rather than the ANC. Forbes says the commission found the police responsible. Al Jazeera likewise raises the politics of selective memory, noting that Langa was largely absent from the national story by 2015.
